turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Mr Adeyemi, in you come. Before Dr Shah's here — blood pressure one hundred and forty-eight over eighty-six, pulse seventy-eight. On the repeat list I've got metformin one gram twice a day, and Lantus thirty-six units at night.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Thirty-six? No. I draw up thirty. Look, I'm knackered, can we not—
[SEG0003] person_3 (DOCTOR): Come through, both of you. I'm Dr Shah. You sound worn out. What's been the main trouble?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): The sugars, I suppose. Work's been stupid, nights and days, I don't even know what—
[SEG0005] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He's up half the night drinking water, his eyes have gone fuzzy, and he gets headaches most evenings. Don't you, love?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Headaches? No I don't. Pack it in. Thirsty, yes. Eyes are a bit off, I'll give you that. Not headaches.
[SEG0007] person_3 (DOCTOR): Alright. Any chest pain, or feeling short of breath?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Nothing like that.
[SEG0009] person_3 (DOCTOR): When did the thirst start?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): It's the warehouse, that's the thing. Late shifts, on my feet till gone eleven. I can't do dates when I'm—
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): The thirst... a couple of weeks, maybe. There. You happy now?
[SEG0012] person_3 (DOCTOR): I am, thank you. What about the feet — numbness, tingling, any sores?
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): Feet are fine. I walk all day, they'd tell me.
[SEG0014] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He's rubbing those toes on the sofa every evening. It's been months.
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): Months? Don't be daft. It's not—
[SEG0016] person_3 (DOCTOR): We'll have a look shortly. The insulin, though — chart says Lantus thirty-six at night, and you've just said thirty.
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): Thirty. They changed it. Last spring, or after Christmas, I can't... I don't remember when.
[SEG0018] person_1 (NURSE): Clinic letter from November still says thirty-six units at night. That's the figure I was reading.
[SEG0019] person_3 (DOCTOR): So the dose doesn't agree, and the date's a blur. I won't change anything today. Are you actually taking it every night?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Not on lates. I get in and I skip it. Two nights, three nights a week, easy.
[SEG0021] person_3 (DOCTOR): And the metformin, one gram morning and evening — that one you take?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah. Breakfast and tea. I don't miss the tablets, just the jab.
[SEG0023] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He misses the morning tablet as well when he's out at five. I've counted them.
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): That's not true. You're thinking of last year. The tablets I take.
[SEG0025] person_3 (DOCTOR): What sort of numbers are you getting on the home meter?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Fasting's been one-eighty-something. Sometimes two-hundred-ish. The screen's tiny and I'm half asleep, so don't pin me down.
[SEG0027] person_1 (NURSE): Finger-prick here was eleven point two, in millimoles. His meter might still be on the American units. I didn't check the device.
[SEG0028] person_3 (DOCTOR): Then one-eighty-something can't go in the notes as a proper reading. Eleven point two here is higher than we'd like. Any shaky spells, hypos?
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I don't get the shakes.
[SEG0030] person_3 (DOCTOR): How long have the eyes been blurry?
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): Few weeks? I dunno. Round when the mornings got lighter. Or before. I can't be doing with this.
[SEG0032] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Since before Easter, that's longer than a few weeks. And the toes are months, I've already said.

[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): Alright, fine. The toes do tingle at night, right foot mostly, worse when I've stood the whole shift, eases a bit with the shoes off. A few weeks, not months, and there's a split in the heel. I said the feet were fine because I didn't want a fuss.
[SEG0034] person_3 (DOCTOR): Thank you for telling me. Any pain in the calves when you're walking?
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Calves are fine. It's just the tingling.
[SEG0036] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): His dad lost a toe with the diabetes. That's why I go on.
[SEG0037] person_3 (DOCTOR): Useful to know. I'll look now.

[SEG0038] person_3 (DOCTOR): Right heel has a shallow crack, the skin's dry, there's no redness and no discharge. Pulses are present in both feet. Monofilament is dull over the right toes and normal on the left.

[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): Can we leave the feet a minute. The drive was a nightmare, roadworks all down the A40 from Greenford, and the cricket was on the radio, England collapsing again before lunch. My grandson kept texting to ask if I'd seen the wicket. I'd sooner have stayed home and watched it.
[SEG0040] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He'll talk about that Test match all week. We had the telly on till midnight Sunday. Lovely weather for the garden as well, completely wasted in a queue.

[SEG0041] person_3 (DOCTOR): Sounds a miserable trek. Coming back to this — the tingling with the reduced feeling, I think that's early nerve damage from the diabetes. Working impression only, not a final label. On timing, since you don't agree, I'll put the blur and the toe tingling down as somewhere between a few weeks and a few months.
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): Type 2 diabetes isn't news. Twelve years. Thirteen, maybe. It's in the notes.

[SEG0043] person_3 (DOCTOR): It is. Bloods today, please — HbA1c, kidney function, and a urine sample for the albumin ratio. I'll also refer you for retinal screening. I'm not guessing at the last eye check.
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): I went. Can't tell you the year. Don't start.
[SEG0045] person_1 (NURSE): I can do the blood and the urine after you finish. Podiatry's got Thursday for the heel if you want it booked.

[SEG0046] person_3 (DOCTOR): Yes, book that podiatry slot. And I'll see you here in four weeks with the results. If the heel goes red, or hot, or starts weeping, don't wait for me — come the same day, here or to A&E.
[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): Four weeks. Right. I'm not promising the meter makes it.

[SEG0048] person_3 (DOCTOR): Bring the meter and the Lantus pen, and try not to skip the night dose after a late shift — leave it by the bed. We'll sort thirty versus thirty-six when we actually see the pen. Go carefully on that A40.

spec.situation: Type 2 diabetic on tablets plus insulin; patient and nurse give different insulin doses, patient skips doses on work days, reads home sugar numbers aloud in a muddled way ('one-eighty-something fasting'). Foot and eye questions.
features: interruptions_trailing_off: people interrupt each other, trail off, or the answer comes two turns after the question.
tangent_small_talk: a long tangent or small talk (traffic, cricket, the weather, a grandchild) that holds NO clinical content; nothing from it is extracted.
relative_speaks_for_patient: a relative answers for the patient and the patient partly contradicts; reported_by follows who said it.

denial_then_admission: the patient first denies a symptom, then later describes it. The label records the symptom as present (the later, fuller answer) and does NOT also record the earlier denial as a negative finding.

bad.reason: Finger-prick glucose was done, but not stated as requested by nurse.
Completed capillary glucose is documented, but nurse not stated responsible for performing it.
bad.text: Capillary glucose already performed (action_type=investigation, status=completed, responsible_person=nurse)

bad.reason: Same-day review instruction is supported, but includes “here or to A&E,” not specifically a doctor consultation.
bad.text: Follow-up consultation (action_type=follow_up, status=conditional, responsible_person=doctor, time_reference=value: if the heel goes red, or hot, or starts weeping, come the same day)

Negative finding asked and answered: patient initially said his feet were fine, denying numbness, tingling, or sores when directly asked.
Negative finding asked and answered: patient denied headaches, despite family member reporting them.
Negative finding asked and answered: patient denied hypos/'the shakes'.

Home glucose meter readings were reported as fasting 'one-eighty-something' and sometimes 'two-hundred-ish', but the clinician explicitly said these should not be entered as proper readings because the meter may be using American units and had not been checked.

Retinal screening referral was planned because the doctor was not willing to guess the date of the last eye check; patient said he had attended previously but could not remember the year.

Self-management advice was more specific than recorded: patient was told to try not to skip the night insulin after a late shift and to leave it by the bed.
